name: Do agrarian states rise and fall in two-to-three-century secular cycles?

positions.claim: Population growth on a fixed land base squeezes peasants, swells and divides the elite, and bankrupts the state; the result is a crisis every two to three centuries.
positions.mech: More people → falling wages and rising rents → more elite aspirants than posts → fiscal crisis → elite factions arm the discontented.
for: Goldstone finds the same sequence before the English, French, Ottoman and Ming crises of the 1640s.
Turchin & Nefedov trace eight cycles in England, France, Rome and Russia with expansion, stagflation, crisis and depression phases.
against: Phase dates are fitted after the fact, and the theory struggles with the timing of any single revolution.
Brenner-school critics say class power, not numbers, decides who wins a crisis.

positions.claim: Before 1800 population pressed on food until famine and plague cut it back; politics followed the demographic tide.
positions.mech: Population outruns land → falling real wages and famine → mortality crisis → recovery of wages.
for: Real wages and population move inversely in England for five centuries.
Le Roy Ladurie found the same long breathing in Languedoc.
against: Wages and population decoupled in the Low Countries and England well before 1800.
Says little about why some crises became revolutions and others did not.

positions.claim: The same demographic shock produced freedom in England and serfdom in Poland, so class structure, not population, explains outcomes.
positions.mech: Shock → contest between lords and organised villages → the stronger side sets the property rules.
for: Opposite outcomes after the Black Death in western and eastern Europe.
against: Hard to measure class power independently of the outcome it is meant to explain.

positions.claim: The great crises line up with cold and drought, which cut harvests just as states were at war.
positions.mech: Cooling or drought → harvest failure and prices → hunger, flight and revolt → state breakdown.
for: The General Crisis of the 1640s hit China, the Ottomans, Russia and Europe in the same cold decades.
Zhang et al. find cold phases matched by war and population decline across 1400-1900.
against: Climate hits everyone; it cannot say why England had a civil war and Japan did not.
Correlations over centuries can hide coincidence.

state: The structural-demographic model is the most tested theory of state breakdown and survives in many cases; the live fight is over whether it predicts or only describes, and how much weight climate shocks carry.
settle: Seshat CrisisDB-style data that code elite numbers, wages and state finances before many crises, compared with matched cases that did not break, ideally scored before the outcome is known.
fun: Turchin predicted in 2010 that the United States would hit peak instability around 2020; whether that counts as a hit is its own debate.

name: Why do complex societies collapse?

positions.claim: Societies solve problems by adding complexity, which costs energy; when each new layer buys less than it costs, collapse is the economical choice.
positions.mech: Problems → more soldiers, officials, taxes → falling marginal return → peasants and provinces opt out → simplification.
for: Late Rome doubled its army and bureaucracy and debased its coin, yet got less security.
The theory covers Rome, the Maya and Chaco with one mechanism.
against: The marginal return of complexity is almost impossible to measure.
Byzantium faced the same costs and lasted a thousand years more.

positions.claim: Societies fail when they damage their environment and do not change course; climate, enemies, trade partners and choices set the outcome.
positions.mech: Five factors: environmental damage, climate change, hostile neighbours, lost trade partners and the society's own responses.
for: Norse Greenland, Chaco and the Maya all fell during droughts or cold on degraded land.
Tokugawa Japan and Tikopia show the same pressures could be managed.
against: Specialists in nearly every case say Diamond overstated self-inflicted damage (Rapa Nui, Norse, Maya).
Questioning Collapse argues many "collapses" were reorganisations.

positions.claim: Abrupt droughts lasting decades, now dated to the year in caves, lakes and trees, broke farming states from Akkad to Angkor.
positions.mech: Multiyear drought → harvest failure and water-system breakdown → war, migration and abandonment.
for: Drought spikes in Maya cave records match waves of abandonment.
Angkor tree rings show megadroughts and floods in the 1300s-1400s.
against: Many droughts left no collapse; timing is often only to decades.
Butzer and Middleton warn against a climate cause for every fall.

positions.school: Collapse is rare; resilience and reorganisation
positions.claim: What looks like the end of a civilisation is usually the end of a ruling class; people, languages and ways of life carry on.
positions.mech: Political breakdown of a centre → dispersal and new forms of order, with continuity for most people.
for: Maya speakers still number millions; Rapa Nui survived until colonial violence.
Middleton finds most textbook collapses were regional and gradual.
against: Ward-Perkins and others show real material losses: smaller cattle, lost literacy, fewer people.

positions.claim: Large states are Goliaths built on extraction by a few; inequality and capture by elites make them fragile, and their fall often frees the many.
positions.mech: Concentrated wealth and power → extraction and bad decisions → fragility to shocks → collapse that often improves commoners' lives.
for: Post-collapse populations often show better health and more equality.
Ties collapse to inequality, as Scheidel ties levelling to collapse.
against: A new, broad synthesis that specialists are still testing case by case.
Collapses also bring mass death, as Ward-Perkins stresses.

state: No single cause wins. Specialists accept climate shocks as real triggers, Tainter's costs as a frame, and insist on human choices and continuity; Diamond's ecocide cases have mostly been revised downward.
settle: Annually dated proxies (ice, caves, tree rings) set against settlement counts and dated destruction across many collapses and near-misses, so triggers can be told from coincidences.
fun: Tainter says collapse can be the rational choice: when the empire costs more than it gives, the peasants simply stop paying for it.

name: Did the Rapa Nui destroy their own world?

positions.claim: Islanders cut down their forest to farm and to move the moai, then starved, fought and fell from perhaps 15,000 to a few thousand before Europeans came.
positions.mech: Statue competition → deforestation → soil loss, no canoes → famine and war → population crash.
for: Pollen cores show the palm forest vanished after settlement.
Toppled statues and obsidian blades were read as signs of war.
against: No dated evidence for a pre-1722 population crash.
Obsidian mata'a are mostly tools, not weapons.

positions.claim: A late-settled, small population adapted to a treeless island with rock gardens and kept building moai; the collapse came after 1722 with disease and slavers.
positions.mech: Rats eat palm seeds → forest loss → lithic mulch farming → stable population → contact diseases and 1862 raids → collapse.
for: Radiocarbon puts settlement near 1200, leaving little time for a long boom and bust.
Rat-gnawed palm nuts are everywhere in the sediments.
against: Rats alone may not explain the speed of forest loss; burning was also heavy.

positions.claim: Satellite mapping finds far less rock gardening than assumed; the island could feed about 3,000 people, which matches what the first Europeans saw.
positions.mech: Garden area → carrying capacity of ~2,000 from gardens, ~3,000 with fish → no room for a crash from 15,000.
for: SWIR imagery plus machine learning maps gardens island-wide.
Ancient genomes show no pre-contact bottleneck.
against: Capacity estimates depend on yield assumptions for sweet potato.

positions.claim: Blaming the islanders recasts a colonial catastrophe (slave raids, smallpox, sheep ranching) as a parable of self-destruction.
positions.mech: Raids and epidemics → population of 111 in 1877 → later observers projected the ruin backward.
for: The 1862-63 raids and their aftermath are well documented.
against: Published in a climate-sceptic journal and polemical in tone.

state: The ecocide story has lost: settlement was late, the population small and stable, and the real collapse followed European contact. Forest loss itself is not in doubt.
settle: More dated household sites and garden ages across the island, and genomic effective-population curves from more ancient individuals.
fun: Islanders likely "walked" the moai upright with ropes, and Hunt and Lipo did it with a replica, so you don't need a forest of rollers to move one.

name: What ended the Late Bronze Age world around 1177 BCE?

positions.claim: Drought, earthquakes, raids, rebellion and broken trade hit an interlocked palace system at once; each alone was survivable, together they were not.
positions.mech: Several shocks → loss of key hubs (Ugarit) → trade in tin, copper and grain fails → cascading palace failure.
for: Destruction layers cluster within decades across Greece, Anatolia, the Levant and Cyprus.
Letters at Ugarit show grain shortages, enemy ships and absent troops at once.
against: Hard to falsify: a list of causes explains everything and nothing.

positions.claim: A 150-year dry spell (the 3.2 ka event) caused famine and migration that set the rest in motion.
positions.mech: Drought → famine → migration and raiding → attacks on palaces.
for: Pollen from the Sea of Galilee and lagoon cores in Cyprus and Syria.
against: Drought timing is approximate and not uniform across the region.

positions.claim: Migrant warrior coalitions, named in Egyptian records, destroyed the coastal kingdoms.
positions.mech: Migration and raids → destruction of cities → collapse of states.
for: Medinet Habu reliefs and texts of Ramesses III; Ugarit's last letters.
against: Sea Peoples look as much like refugees and symptoms as causes.

positions.claim: Infantry with javelins and long swords made chariot armies obsolete, so raiders could beat palace kings.
positions.mech: New infantry tactics → chariot armies defeated → palaces sacked.
for: Naue II swords and new armour spread at the right time.
against: Weak evidence that chariots were ever beaten this way; most specialists doubt it.

positions.claim: A swarm of earthquakes over decades damaged many palaces.
positions.mech: Fault rupture sequence → building collapse → weakened states.
for: Crushed skeletons and tilted walls at Mycenae and Tiryns.
against: Cities recover from earthquakes; quakes alone cannot explain abandonment.

state: Most specialists now accept a multicausal systems collapse with drought as a key stress; Cline's sequel stresses that Phoenicia, Assyria and Cyprus adapted and some thrived.
settle: Tighter radiocarbon and dendro dates for each destruction layer, and local climate records near each site, to see what came first.
fun: The end of one world invented the next: the alphabet and iron spread in the gap the palaces left.

name: Do empires rise from frontier solidarity and die of luxury?

positions.claim: Group feeling forged in hard desert or mountain life lets a tribe conquer cities; within about four generations luxury dissolves it and a new tribe takes over.
positions.mech: Harsh frontier → cohesion (asabiyya), doubled by religion → conquest → urban luxury → decline → replacement.
for: The Maghreb sequence Almoravid, Almohad, Marinid follows the script.
Arab conquerors beat far larger Persian and Roman armies at Qadisiyya and Yarmuk.
against: Built from North African cases; dynasties elsewhere often last far longer than four generations.

positions.claim: Empires arise on frontiers between very different peoples, where pressure selects for cohesive groups; Russia, Rome and the Ottomans began there.
positions.mech: Intense intergroup conflict → cultural selection for cooperation → expansion → cohesion decays in the safe core.
for: Most Old World megaempires formed on the steppe frontier.
Muscovy grew on the Tatar frontier.
against: Frontiers also produce endless small states; the theory picks its winners after the fact.

positions.claim: Steppe empires were not rival civilisations built on cohesion but parasites that formed to extort a unified China and fell when China fell.
positions.mech: Chinese unification → steppe confederation to extract trade and tribute → both rise and fall together.
for: Xiongnu rose with the Han; the Turks with the Sui and Tang.
against: Does not explain the Mongols, who conquered rather than extorted.

positions.claim: Early frontier states like the Ottomans held together through shared booty and mixed alliances, not purity of faith or kin.
positions.mech: Successful raiding → recruits from all sides → state-building.
for: Christian lords and converts among early Ottoman commanders.
against: Religion and holy-war language still mattered to contemporaries.

state: Ibn Khaldun remains the founding text of this field; Turchin turned asabiyya into testable models with mixed results, and Ottoman historians replaced the ghaza thesis with plunder coalitions.
settle: A cohesion measure (marriage, oath, shared ritual) coded for polities before and after their rise, compared with frontier groups that never built empires.
fun: Ibn Khaldun gave a dynasty four generations: the builder, the one who knew the builder, the imitator and the destroyer.

name: How does a society escape the war of all against all?

positions.claim: A roving bandit who settles down has an interest in his victims' prosperity; order begins as the self-interest of the strongest thief.
positions.mech: Encompassing interest → limited taxation and protection → more output to tax → state.
for: Olson's example: Chinese warlords like Feng Yuxiang were welcomed over roving bandits.
against: Says little about why some autocrats plunder anyway, or about political legitimacy.

positions.claim: Most societies are natural states where elites share rents to stop fighting; a few crossed to open access after meeting doorstep conditions.
positions.mech: Elite rent-sharing pact → rule of law for elites, perpetual organisations, civilian control of army → open entry.
for: Britain, France and the US crossed between about 1800 and 1900.
After 1688 the English crown borrowed cheaply.
against: Descriptive categories; hard to say when a country has crossed.

positions.claim: States grew to fight wars; the need for money and soldiers built bureaucracies, taxes and bargains with subjects.
positions.mech: Military competition → extraction → bureaucracy and representation.
for: Warring States China and early modern Europe both produced centralised states.
against: Africa and Latin America had wars without strong states; Hui shows war can also produce empire, not a state system.

positions.claim: Order needs three things in balance: a strong impersonal state (China had it first), law that binds rulers, and accountable government.
positions.mech: Kinship → war and state-building → institutional balance or repatrimonialisation.
for: Qin built a merit-based state in the third century BCE.
Mamluk and Ottoman slave-soldier systems were ways around kin.
against: Grand synthesis built on secondary literature; regional specialists contest details.

positions.school: States are not the only order
positions.claim: Early states were fragile grain-and-captive machines; people often fled them, and many large societies organised themselves without kings.
positions.mech: Grain taxation and coercion → fragility → collapse or escape; alternatives through assemblies and seasonal politics.
for: Teotihuacan built housing, not palaces, for centuries.
Early Mesopotamian states repeatedly collapsed.
against: Archaeological readings of egalitarian cities are contested; violence rates in stateless societies were often high.

state: Bellicist and limited-access accounts dominate political economy; Olson's bandit is a classic thought experiment; Scott and Graeber & Wengrow have reopened whether order requires a state at all.
settle: Comparisons of homicide, taxation and settlement before and after state formation in many regions, from Seshat-style data on violence and institutions.
fun: Olson's point: a bandit who stays is better than one who leaves, because he wants you rich enough to rob again next year.

name: Do institutions explain why some nations are rich and others poor?

positions.claim: Nations prosper when institutions spread power and protect property widely; extractive ones, often colonial, keep them poor.
positions.mech: Critical junctures (plague, colonisation, revolution) + small institutional differences → diverging paths that persist.
for: The two Koreas.
Mita districts in Peru are poorer today than villages just outside.
Settler mortality predicts institutions and income.
against: Settler mortality data were challenged by Albouy.
China grew fast under extractive institutions.
Explanations fitted after the fact.

positions.claim: Climate, disease burden and access to the sea shape income directly, not only through institutions.
positions.mech: Malaria and tropical soils, landlocked location → low productivity and costly trade.
for: Tropical and landlocked countries are poorer on average.
against: Reversal of fortune: rich places in 1500 became poor, which geography alone cannot explain.

positions.claim: Schooling and good policies drive growth, and institutions improve afterwards; the usual institution measures capture outcomes, not constraints.
positions.mech: Education → growth → democracy and secure property.
for: South Korea and Taiwan grew under dictatorship.
against: Education itself depends on institutions.

positions.claim: The Great Enrichment came from a change in how people talked about trade and innovation, not from new rules.
positions.mech: Bourgeois revaluation → honour for innovators → mass innovation.
for: Institutions like property rights existed long before 1700 in many places.
against: Rhetoric is hard to measure; why Holland and Britain?

positions.claim: Britain and the Yangzi delta were alike until 1750; cheap coal, high wages and American land made Britain different.
positions.mech: Factor prices and resource windfalls → incentive to mechanise.
for: Steam engines paid only where coal was cheap and labour dear.
against: Underplays institutions and science; British wages and coal were themselves outcomes.

state: Institutions are the mainstream answer in economics, sharpened by natural experiments like the mita and Korea; critics have won the point that geography, human capital and resources interact with them.
settle: More natural experiments with sharp boundaries, and long panels where institutions change without income changing first.
fun: The same people on either side of the 38th parallel: in 2000 one side had famine and the other made smartphones.

name: Does only catastrophe level inequality?

positions.claim: For five thousand years only mass-mobilisation war, transformative revolution, state failure and lethal pandemic have sharply reduced inequality.
positions.mech: Violent shock → destroys capital or makes labour scarce → lower inequality.
for: Post-Black Death wages, the Great Compression after 1945, Soviet and Chinese revolutions, post-Roman and post-Mycenaean simplicity.
against: Policy-driven levelling in Scandinavia and Latin America (2000s).
Some plagues did not level.

positions.claim: Taxation, unions and schooling explain much of the twentieth-century compression; the wars mattered because of the policies they made possible.
positions.mech: Political choices about tax, wages and education → lower inequality.
for: US wage compression stayed after controls ended.
Top income shares responded to tax rates.
against: The big policy shifts came during or after wars, as Scheidel says.

positions.claim: The Black Death levelled, but later plagues did not, because elites adapted inheritance and property law.
positions.mech: Mortality shock × institutions → levelling or not.
for: Tax records from Italian towns, 1300-1800.
against: Evidence mostly from Italy and the Low Countries.

positions.claim: Inequality rises and falls in waves driven by technology, globalisation and politics; wars are one of several "malign" forces among benign ones.
positions.mech: Technological change and trade raise inequality; politics, education and war bring it down.
for: Long waves in the US and UK since 1800.
against: Waves are hard to forecast.

state: Scheidel's historical pattern is widely accepted as a description; the argument is whether peaceful levelling is possible, with the 1930s-70s policy record and Alfani's plague evidence on the other side.
settle: Long series of wealth shares from many societies before and after shocks of different kinds, separating violence from the policies it triggered.
fun: Scheidel's grim joke: if you want equality, history offers four ways to get it, and all of them kill millions.

name: What does the Seshat databank show about the road to big societies, and did big gods come first?

positions.claim: Across 414 polities in 30 regions, size, hierarchy, government, money and writing rise together, so societies grow along one main axis.
positions.mech: Scale and institutions co-evolve; one principal component explains about three-quarters of the variation.
for: The first principal component of Seshat variables explains most of the variance in all regions.
against: Coding choices and the 30-region sample shape the result.

positions.school: War and military technology drive scale
positions.claim: Among the tested drivers, military technology (iron, cavalry) and agricultural productivity best predict the growth of social complexity.
positions.mech: Arms races between polities → selection for larger, more organised societies.
for: Iron and horse spread precedes jumps in polity size across Seshat.
against: Correlational; competing proxies for religion and trade are coarse.

positions.claim: Moralizing high gods appeared only after societies reached about a million people.
positions.mech: Large, anonymous societies → need for supernatural policing to keep cooperation.
for: Seshat time series in 12 regions.
against: Missing data had been coded as absence of belief; the paper was retracted in 2021.
Historians said early texts already show moralising gods.

positions.school: Big gods helped make big societies
positions.claim: Belief in watching, punishing gods helped strangers trust each other; with missing data handled properly, Seshat cannot show complexity came first.
positions.mech: Supernatural monitoring → cooperation among strangers → larger groups.
for: Beheim et al. re-analysis.
In Austronesia, broad supernatural punishment preceded political complexity.
Ibn Khaldun: religion doubled the asabiyya of the Arab conquerors.
against: Watts et al. found high moralizing gods followed complexity in Austronesia.

positions.claim: Early cities and kingdoms show many forms of order, including large egalitarian towns; complexity is not one ladder.
positions.mech: Political choice and seasonal experimentation produce varied institutions.
for: Teotihuacan housing, Ukrainian mega-sites, Tlaxcala's council.
against: Statistical regularities in Seshat still need explaining.

state: Seshat showed strong regularities in how societies scale; the moralizing-gods paper was retracted, and the order of gods and complexity is open again. Whitehouse and colleagues published a revised analysis in 2023.
settle: Coding protocols that separate "absent" from "unknown", and early written or archaeological evidence of supernatural punishment for more regions.
fun: A Nature paper on gods and empires was retracted because blanks in a spreadsheet had been read as "no gods".

name: What broke Rome: plague and climate, or Huns and Goths?

positions.claim: Pandemics and a cooling climate ended the Roman boom: lead in Greenland ice falls off a cliff in 165 and recovers only around 750.
positions.mech: Pandemic mortality and cold → fewer taxpayers, soldiers and miners → fiscal and military crisis.
for: Lead emissions tracked plague, war and expansion year by year.
The 536 cooling and the Justinianic plague hit the eastern empire.
against: Haldon and colleagues: palaeoclimate and plague evidence too coarse to carry the causal weight.
Mordechai et al. call the Justinianic Plague inconsequential.

positions.claim: The Hunnic push of 376 set barbarian groups loose inside the empire; losing Africa's taxes broke the West.
positions.mech: Huns → Goths cross Danube → Adrianople → sack of Rome → loss of tax provinces → no army.
for: Ammianus and the narrative sources; the timing of losses of Gaul, Spain and Africa.
against: The East faced the same barbarians and survived.

positions.claim: The fall was not a gentle transformation: living standards in the West dropped to prehistoric levels.
positions.mech: End of state and army → end of specialisation and trade → material collapse.
for: Pottery, coins, building and cattle size all drop after 400.
against: Focus on the West, especially Britain; the East and Near East prospered.

positions.claim: Late Antiquity was a creative age of new religions, art and states, not a fall.
positions.mech: Reorganisation of culture and power around churches, holy men and new kingdoms.
for: Flourishing Christian, Jewish and Islamic cultures between 250 and 750.
against: Underplays violence and material loss in the West.

positions.claim: Papyri, laws, coins and pollen show no sign of mass mortality after 541; the environmental story is overdrawn.
positions.mech: Pandemics were real but their demographic and political effects were limited.
for: Continuity in land use and legislation after 541.
against: Ancient DNA confirms Yersinia pestis across Europe in the sixth century.

state: Heather's external shock is the standard narrative for the West, and Ward-Perkins won the argument that the fall hurt; Harper's environmental history is influential but contested, and the Greenland lead record is the strongest new evidence for a second-century turning point.
settle: Ice-core, tree-ring and ancient-DNA records with annual dates set against dated coin hoards, mines and settlement counts in each province.
fun: Roman miners left a fingerprint in Greenland ice: you can see the Antonine Plague as a drop in lead pollution 4,000 km away.
